- When sentiment is consistently bullish (≥0.67) and model forecasts are flat or rising slowly, expect overshoot or overconfidence; adjust downward if true outcome shows sharp decline or mean reversion.
- If recent events show high bearish net supply (e.g., >15 events, net < -10), model tends to overestimate recovery; reduce forecast slope or add downward bias.
- After a sharp spike in price (e.g., >10% from prior 5-day avg), model often overcorrects; cap forecast rise to 3–5% per period unless sentiment strongly bullish.
- If sentiment history shows repeated 0.00 or negative values (e.g., -0.33), model may ignore bearish signals; force a 2–5% downward adjustment if true outcome confirms bearish trend.
- When official event count is high and supply net is negative, model tends to overestimate price stability; apply mean reversion bias toward recent 7-day average if true outcome diverges.
- If model forecast is rising steadily but true outcome shows early dip (e.g., first 5 days), reduce forecast slope by 10–20% to account for lag or sentiment reversal.
- For high event count with bullish sentiment, model may overestimate upside; cap forecast at 10–15% above recent 10-day high unless sentiment is strongly bullish (≥0.8).
- If sentiment history shows alternating 0.33/1.00, model may misinterpret trend; use weighted average of sentiment and price history to smooth forecast.
